What Is Medicine?
●
In the early 20th Century as China was going through a reform, intellectuals were 
questioning Chinese traditions as they felt they were holding China’s growth. They 
wanted to do things the Western way.
○
Chen Yin Ke: “Effective medication but theories lack coherence”.
○
Chinese intellectuals were abandoning Chinese medicine because it contains the
5 elements, the 6 qi, and were thought to be superstitious.
○
Assumption that science was purely a Western product, and could not be found 
in Chinese traditions.
●
In the present day, we prefer Western clinics as we trust their medical interpretations of 
our illness — since it is backed by science.
●
Modern medicine (Western medicine) is based on observing and seeing.
●
In the past, fundamental theories of the human body cannot have arisen solely from 
observation of the body. It requires a model external to the body (life experience in 
actual or desired living environment). — MEDICINE IS CLOSELY RELATED TO 
CULTURE.
●
Consciousness / qi is what is necessary for life, it is the immaterial aspect of our body.
●
Emergence of medicine allowed one to recognise early processes in the body as 
“pathological”. Physicians can predict how these processes develop to cause illness.
●
Aim of medicine is to preserve life. To do so, it uses the scientific study of nature — 
nature of man and his habitat — applicable to people of all nationalities and religions.
Beginnings
●
Many ancient cultures shared the common belief that causes of illnesses were related to
the head.
●
Trepanning  — an operation to expel evil spirits from the head — was an early type of 
healing in the West, NOT used by the Chinese.
●
The Chinese knew that the dampness from living in caves was causing them illnesses, 
so they tried to modify the environment (building houses). If they could not modify the 
environment successfully, they would relocate to other places.
●
This developed a culture of hygiene, which was essential for the development of 
medicine.
●
People began shifting from collective representation to their individual, as they started to 
realise that there was a gap between life and death, and that only their soul was 
immortal.
●
During the Shang Dynasty, the Chinese believed that dead ancestors’ 
displeasure were the cause of illness. The healers were the priests and the 
King. Most powerful cosmological force was 帝.
●
During the Zhou Dynasty, the healers became the witches / shamans (巫). 
People switched to worshipping heaven (天). Power of the ancestors was now 
shared with other spirits who could make things difÏcult for the living. Trying

●
During the Qin-Han Dynasty, the concept of spirits (神) was redefined. Blood 
and 气 combine to form the spirits of the body. 神 became closely related to 
the mind.
○
脏 is tied to spirits, and they are long-term storage organs of the body.
○
腑 are short-term storage organs of the body, not tied to spirits.
○
神 is maintained if there is a healthy balance of 气 in the 脏.
○
Spirits are maintained through emotions (BALANCED, NOT EXTREME 
EMOTIONS): joy, anger, worry, grief, fear, fright and pensiveness (七情).
Spirits are now under human control, not the other way around.
○
Organs can be repleted (實) or depleted (虚).
Natural Philosophy and Chinese Medicine
●
Natural order was timeless. Thinkers started to view humans as intricately connected to 
nature. Humans should also follow the natural order and not try to change things.
●
During the Warring States period, philosophy of the demons broke down, instead 
focussing on Yin-Yang, the five elements and Qi. This marked the beginning of natural 
philosophy in China.
●
Integration of natural philosophy into Chinese medicine.
阴阳
●
Yin-Yang: opposite, yet complementary forces.
●
The natural philosophy can be used to explain forces of nature. E.g. the Yin-Yang 
concept was known for the creation of the world.

The Theory of The Five Elements (
 
 五行
 
 ) 
●
Originated from The Five Virtues 五德终始说, each representing an element — 
metal, wood, water, fire and earth.
●

●
The five phases are interconnected and associated with mutual generation and 
destruction.
○
Water: Potential of new life under water in winter.
○
Wood: Exuberance of new growth in spring.
○
Fire: Process of maturation under warmth of summer sun.
○
Earth: Ripening of grains in late summer.
○
Metal: Harvest of autumn, storage of seeds for next year’s planting, beginning of
new cycle.
●
The generation / production of phases is one where each element generates the 
element after it — mutual generation.
●
There are also checks in place to ensure the elements are balanced — mutual control / 
restraint.
●
If there is imbalance, there will be destruction. The destructive cycle occurs 
when an element becomes too strong from its control element and uses up 
all its energy (气).
○
Earth absorbs water, water extinguishes fire, fire melts metal, metal cuts wood, 
wood breaks earth.
Organs & Meridians In Classical Medical Texts
●
Authorship of 黄帝内经 is unknown. It is a compilation of several fragmentary 
texts of several authors.
●
Date of completion is unknown. First book written no earlier than 4th century B.C. 
completed in 3rd century A.D.
●
黄帝内经 was finalised in paper book form and widely circulated by the Song 
Dynasty. It was divided into 2 parts: 素问 (Basic Questions or Inquiry into the 
Fundamental) and 灵枢 (discusses acupuncture in great detail).
○
Acupuncture needles are inserted in acupoints along meridian channels.
●
Health and disease are influenced by natural ageing processes and the environment.

●
Body also consists of meridian organs (经络) — consists of meridian channels 
(经脉) and associated vessels or collaterals (络脉).

Chinese Medicine From Medieval to Late Imperial Period
From Han To Tang
●
Medical texts from Mawangdui wrote that spirits were to be blamed as the perpetrators 
of diseases. There was no mention of Yin-Yang, or Five Phases, nor the natural laws 
that the body needs to follow — signifying that they all appeared from a great revolution.
●
In the past there was a huge rift between drug therapy and acupuncture.
○
Drug therapy is the use of plant and animal-based medicine for treatment.
○
Drugs were associated with witchcraft, thus the elite didn’t like it.
○
Many prescriptions were recorded in 伤寒论, which also combined ideas
of systematic correspondence.
●
Transformation of Daoism into a religion at the end of the Han dynasty.
●
Pursuit of immortality led to the pursuit of using herbs in Chinese medicine — drug 
therapy became slowly accepted.
●
Drug therapy became a major therapeutic method in Chinese medicine by the end of the
Song dynasty.
●
Buddhism came into China from India, and was redefined to fit local cultures. This also 
influenced Chinese medicine.
○
Important causes of diseases (三病).
○
Mediation techniques became important, resembling breathing exercises from 
the Mawangdui.
○
Government set up a ministry for research into medicine (in the Sui dynasty).
●
Peace and stability of the early Tang dynasty encouraged innovation. Daoist influence 
was still dominant in Chinese medicine.

Song-Jin-Yuan
●
Song emperors were proficient in drug therapy and Chinese medicine.
●
The elites in China transformed from “men of good birth” to “men of culture”.
○
In the past, state positions were given to the wealthy landowners, making one’s 
fate determined by one’s wealth instead of merit.
○
It changed to imperial examinations to find officials from both noble and base 
families — more meritocratic.
○
The Song emperors saw the education and examination system as reordering 
society and transforming the elite.
○
Development of Confucianism — influenced by Daoism and Buddhism.
●
Medicine became popular among the scholars, worthy of their time and energy. They 
shaped how physicians studied and practised medicine, as they decided which medical 
texts were to be printed and circulated.
●
Printing became cheaper, allowing for higher circulation of texts (identical ones). This led
to the democratisation of medical knowledge.
●
Government bureau is set up to correct errors in medical texts which are 
published. This included editing 伤寒论, a text that was widely forgotten but 
important for dealing with epidemics.
○
Circulation of books on drug therapy with more formulas and explanations for 
each illness, increased the prestige of drug therapy.
●
By the end of the Song, the physician was no longer any healer, but a cultured scholar 
who had moral and social responsibility.
●
Medical reforms of the Song dynasty. The government began to view healthcare as its 
responsibility (provided by charity institutions in the past).
○
Setting up of hospitals and pharmacies.
○
Subsidise medical drugs.
●
New focus on the dynamics of qi transformation and how its breakdown led to
证.
○
Factors: Yin and Yang, external and internal, hot and cold, excess and 
deficiency.
○
Also influenced by the environment, body constitution of patients and the medical
disorder.
Becoming ‘Traditional Chinese Medicine’
●
Transmission of Chinese medical knowledge to Europe during the 16th Century.
●
At the end of the imperial age, China began embracing Western medicine.
○
Western medical texts were also being translated to Manchu language and 
brought into China.
●
Chinese medicine was revitalised post-1949, and transmitted to the West.
●
Western scholars noted that Chinese medicine focussed on pulse instead of urine.
○
Read Chinese medical texts too literally, thus feeling that they were empirical 
medicine (not based on concrete scientific evidence).

Chinese Medicine in Singapore
●
Chinese medicine in everyday life: drinking coconut water after vaccines, traditional 
chinese veterinary medicine, different chinese medicine being sold.
●
Why are we using TCM? Effective to many people, avoiding side effects of biomedicine.
●
In the past, locals were mainly reliant on TCM for treatment, but now, we have 
transitioned to using Western medicine.
○
In the past, TCM provided charity treatment for the poor, boosting the role of 
TCM in society in the past.
○
No licensing of TCM physicians — selecting physicians based on examinations, 
like in China.
○
The Chinese Medicine physicians brought the culture from China to Singapore.
●
Localisation and adaptation of TCM in Singapore:
○
In the present, TCM cannot be integrated with biomedicine by law.
○
Halal-certified Chinese herbs. More Malays seeking TCM treatments.
○
More research into how ethnic differences can affect effectiveness of TCM 
treatment.
●
Gaining credibility:
○
State support allowed TCM to gain credibility.
○
TCM is seen as a complementary medicine — primarily focuses on prevention.
○
Non-state actors (Singapore Chinese Physicians' Association, etc.) include 
research and charity halls. They reach out to all races.
●

○
TB: Caused by external climatic factors (summer heat, dampness, fire) 
and internal emotions (七情) (anger, worry, anxiety, sadness, fear,

Comparison With Malay Medicine
●
Similarities:
○
Focus on interconnectedness of organs in the body, and humans and the

○
Concepts of energy, mind, and spirit.
○
Balance among different elements (water, earth, air, fire), deficiency and excess.
○
Hot / cold, damp / dry dichotomies.
○
Also use similar treatments: Herbs, food as medicine, acupressure, bone setting, 
cupping, incantations and rituals.
○
Particular time, frequency, direction, position, number to take medication.
○
Also related to the religious world view of the community.
●
Differences:

TCM In Hong Kong
●
In the 1850s herbal shops began setting up in Hong Kong, and by 1872, the first TCM 
hospital (TWH) was set up in Hong Kong to provide Chinese medicine treatment.
○
During the plague, TWH introduced Western medicine.
○
After that, people began to lose confidence in Chinese medicine. Western 
medicine became the mainstream of Medicine.
○
Chinese medicine services shrank even further during the Japanese Occupation.
The Japanese government ordered the closure of free TCM clinics, and only 
offered free Western medicine clinics.
●
Southward migration of Chinese scholars and practitioners to Hong Kong accelerated 
TCM development.
●
After 1997, the government recognised Chinese medicine (exams for practitioners, 
university programs for Chinese medicine).
●
During SARS, Chinese medicine practitioners collaborated with their mainland 
counterparts. — FIRST integration between Chinese and Western medicine.
○
CM was recognised to treat SARS.

The Art & Science of Traditional Chinese Medicine Diagnostics
●
TCM treatment process: 
○
Identify the underlying patterns of disharmony, in a process called syndrome 
differentiation.
○
Diagnose the disease, matching disease and syndrome to customise 
individualised treatments to fit the patient’s unique presentation.
○
MORE PATIENT-CENTRED, focus on OVERALL BALANCE.
○
Same illness can lead to different treatments based on different body 
constitutions.
●
How does TCM diagnostics work?
○
Knowing the interior through the exterior.
○
Recognising the whole through observing a part — observing the tongue, feeling 
the pulse, diagnosing through acupoints.
○
Knowing the norm to identify change — consider Yin-Yang balance, spirit-body-
mind balance, environment, societal factors.
●
Restores the whole balance, not just targets the symptom. 
●
Principles of TCM diagnostics:
○
Holistic examination: Consider the disease causes, disease history, dynamic 
changes of Yin, Yang, Qi and blood, body constitution, family, environment, 
seasonal and climatic changes.
○
Synthesis of different diagnostics: Pay equal attention to all 4 diagnostic 
information and collect complete medical data.
○
Combination of disease and syndrome: Disease focuses on cause, mechanism, 
progression, and outcome. Syndrome studies the body’s reaction in its current

Acupuncture
●
Involves insertion of needles at acupoints (along the meridian system).
●
Regulates elements (Yin, Yang, Qi, blood) and ensures smoother coordination between 
organs.
●
3 angles for acupuncture:
○
Flat needling: For areas with shallow skin (head / chest). Angle of entry = 15°.
○
Inclined needling: For areas with shallow muscles (neck / throat). Angle of entry =
45°.
○
Straight needling: For areas with thick muscles (limbs / lower back). Angle of 
entry = 90°.

Chinese Ideas of Health Preservation & Ageing
●
TCM holds that humans are one with heaven and earth and the natural environment.
●
Health preservation is concerned with maintaining health, preventing illness, and 
extending life span. 
○
Cultivate body, mind, character, spirit.
○
Cultivate jing, qi and shen.
○
The mind is the starting point of preserving health.
○
7 emotions are the activities of the mind: joy, anger, sorrow, fear, love, hate, 
desire. Ensure they are in balance and do not become excessive (prevents 
illness).
○
Emotions are linked to zang-fu organs. Ability to regulate these emotions are 
related to the state of Qi and blood in these organs, and body constitution.
●
BOTH body and mind: body have to be active, mind have to be quiet — BALANCE.
